summary: On 21 October 2016 a distributed denial-of-service attack on the DNS provider Dyn, partly from devices infected with the Mirai botnet, made many popular sites unreachable for users on the US East Coast. Dyn described it as sophisticated and highly distributed, involving tens of millions of IP addresses.

overview.background: Dyn provided DNS for many large sites. DNS turns names into addresses, so if the provider is unreachable, names stop resolving even though the sites themselves are up.
systems: Customers using Dyn as their DNS provider
overview.impact: Users on the US East Coast reaching Dyn servers could not access some customer sites. Dyn said it did not have a system-wide outage.
overview.severity: Two attack waves with service restored around 1:00 pm ET, per the report.
overview.gaps: The Dyn analysis page (the card source) was not read. Details come from a trade-press report of Dyn's statements.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

diagrams.title: Attack on the DNS provider hides many sites
diagrams.caption: Per the report, Dyn was hit in waves by a highly distributed attack. Sites that used Dyn as their DNS provider could not be reached from affected regions.

nodes.label: Dyn DNS servers overwhelmed in waves
Customer sites unreachable in affected regions

diagrams.title: More than one DNS provider (conceptual)
diagrams.caption: A general design: use two independent DNS providers so one attack does not hide your names.

afterChanges: Names resolve if one provider fails.
Failures are seen from several regions.
Recovery does not depend on one vendor.
afterNote: The after picture shows the corrective ideas in the source and general good practice. It is conceptual unless the source says otherwise.
timelineNote: Times are as published by the source. Entries without a clock time are given in order only.

timeline.e: A second, more global wave hits.
Dyn mitigates the second wave; service is restored around 1:00 pm ET.
Dyn verifies an attempted third wave, mitigated without customer impact.
Dyn confirms Mirai-based botnets as a main source of attack traffic.

rootCause.trigger: A highly distributed attack, in part from Mirai-infected devices, overwhelmed Dyn's DNS service.
rootCause.underlying: Many sites used Dyn as their only DNS provider.
contributing: The card also notes resolver retries added load; the report read does not mention retries

evidence.label: Dyn's description
evidence.note: From the report of Dyn's statement.

evidence.label: Scope of outage
evidence.body: Dyn did not experience a system-wide outage at any time

diagnose.step: Check if your names resolve from several regions.
Check which DNS provider you use.
diagnose.why: A single provider is a single point of failure.

correct.step: Use short time to live and cached fallbacks where possible.

fix.safety: Changing DNS records or name servers during an attack can extend the outage. Plan and test before you need to.

troubleshoot.scenario: Your site is up but users in some regions cannot resolve your names. Your only DNS provider is under attack.
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
hints: What should you have set up?
troubleshoot.answer: Wait for the provider if you must, but add a second provider, update name servers with care and communicate. Long term, run two providers.

rootcause.q: What did Dyn say about the attack?

design.prompt: Design DNS for a global consumer service.
design.answer: Two independent providers, automated sync, anycast, monitoring and runbooks.

checks.q: When did the first wave begin?
Did Dyn say it had a system-wide outage?
How many waves did Dyn verify?
options: Three, with the third mitigated without impact

sources.title: Channel Futures: Dyn: DDoS Attack Involved 10s of Millions of IP Addresses

verification: Facts were read on 29 October 2026 from a trade-press report of Dyn's statements. Dyn's own analysis page could not be read. The card says resolver retries added load; the report does not mention retries, so the root cause lists it only as the card's claim.
